analysis.one_liner: Cuts off federal energy aid to investor-owned utilities that raise home electric rates.
analysis.headline: The bill has one cosponsor and has sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee since its referral, with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tells the Secretary of Energy to stop giving money to regulated investor-owned electric utilities that charge homeowners more for electricity than they did on January 1, 2026. For the first year, any rate hike above that date's level means no federal financial assistance, and a utility already receiving assistance that hikes rates has it cut off. For the next two years, a utility can raise rates above that level only if it cuts the total pay of its five highest-paid executives by twice the size of the rate increase and reports the numbers to the Energy Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Households facing rising electric bills, in states served by investor-owned utilities that receive or would seek Energy Department financial assistance. The bill uses the department's money as leverage: keep home rates at early-2026 levels or lose the aid. It also aims any cost of higher rates back at utility executives, whose pay must fall by twice the rate increase if rates rise.

how_it_helps.text: For one year, no utility regulated by a state and owned by investors may receive Department of Energy financial assistance if it charges residential customers more than its January 1, 2026 rate [S2].
A utility receiving assistance during that year that raises residential rates must have that assistance terminated by the Secretary [S2].

For two more years, a rate increase above the January 1, 2026 level is allowed only if the utility cuts the total compensation — salary, bonuses, stock awards, stock options, and other pay — of its five highest-paid employees by twice the percentage-point rate increase, and files a report with the Secretary [S2].
Violating the executive pay condition during the later period also triggers termination of the assistance [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Investor-owned electric utilities that want federal energy money. To keep it, they must hold home rates at early-2026 levels, or accept a proportional cut in executive pay and extra reporting. Utilities that raise rates anyway lose the federal assistance. Ratepayers could still see rates set higher by their state regulator if the utility is willing to give up federal money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investor-owned electric utilities seeking federal aid

drawbacks.text: The bill only reaches utilities in line for Department of Energy financial assistance; a utility that raises rates and simply forgoes federal aid is untouched, and the actual rates are set by state regulators [S2].
Freezing rates at January 1, 2026 levels could lock in rates that were already high before that date [S2].

A hard rate ceiling can squeeze utility budgets; a good-faith objection is that holding rates flat while fuel and infrastructure costs rise can leave less for grid maintenance, pushing costs off to later years.
Enforcement depends entirely on the Secretary of Energy determining a violation and choosing to terminate assistance [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is narrow but pointed: it does not set national rates, it makes federal money conditional on keeping home rates from rising, and it attaches the cost of any increase to executive pay rather than to customers. Its main limits are that state regulators actually set rates, utilities can walk away from federal aid, and a freeze pegged to January 2026 can preserve rates that were already high. It is a modest affordability lever, not a broad rate cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it so far.

narrative.text: Rep. Haley Stevens introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1].
It has one cosponsor, a Democrat [S3].
The complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote recorded [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has lost anything — the bill simply sits in committee. Investor-owned utilities are better off for now because the rate-and-pay conditions have not advanced toward law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities, for now — the bill has not moved

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's sole cosponsor [S3].

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats are on the bill and no Republican has engaged with it, so no partisan division has formed yet.

industries.note: The bill makes federal Energy Department assistance conditional on holding residential rates at January 2026 levels and, after the first year, on cutting top executives' pay by twice any rate increase. The utilities' financial interest in raising rates runs directly against ratepayers' interest in stable bills.
The five highest-paid executives at a utility that raises rates must absorb a pay cut worth twice the rate increase, with pay defined to include salary, bonuses, stock awards, and stock options [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, one cosponsor, and no committee action in months, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote in this Congress; most bills referred to committee never advance that far. It could gain traction only if electricity prices became a major issue and it attracted many more cosponsors.
